# Swarming Support

`customer_support.model.swarming_support` · model · parent `—`

> No tiers. A contact is owned end to end by whoever picks it up, and when that person cannot finish it they convene the people who can — synchronously, in the open — rather than passing it upward. The structural claim is that handoffs, not skill gaps, are what make support slow: every transfer re-reads the ticket, re-asks the customer, and re-decides what was already decided. Swarming pays for that with senior attention spent on ordinary tickets, and the entire question of whether the model works is whether the interruptions cost less than the handoffs did. . What breaks structurally is the escalation ladder. There is no tier-2 queue to escalate INTO, so "escalated within two hours" — a clause that appears in a great many support contracts — has no referent here. Commercial and support leadership routinely discover this after signing. . What an operator carries over wrongly from a tiered org: per-agent throughput. When five people touch one resolution, tickets-per-agent-per-day measures nothing, first-contact resolution by agent measures less, and a manager reading last quarter's dashboard will see a productivity collapse in month one and kill the model in month three. The unit of measurement has to move from the agent to the resolution before the model is switched on, not after.


## Characteristics

|  |  |
|---|---|
| requester | the same mix as the canonical motion — swarming changes who answers, never who asks |
| typical_resolution_hours | 6 |
| volume_shape | moderate volume, high variance in difficulty; the tail is what swarming attacks |
| staffing_model | flat pool with published skill tags; work is claimed, never routed upward |
| coverage | single region or overlapping regions — a swarm needs people awake at the same time |
| automation_level | low to moderate; deflection sits in front of the pool, not inside it |
| primary_channels | `ticket_portal`, `email`, `chat` |
| notes | Swarming has a hard prerequisite most adopters skip: the swarm's reasoning has to land somewhere durable. If the resolution lives in the chat channel where it happened, nothing was learned, and the same four people reconvene on the same problem the following week. A swarming org without a functioning knowledge motion is just an expensive tiered org.  |

## Extends `customer_support.obj.core.ticket`

Requires `assignee`, `status`


> The assignee is the accountable human for the life of the ticket and does not change when help arrives. This is the one invariant of the model — the moment reassignment becomes normal, the swarm has quietly reinvented tier two with worse bookkeeping.


## Extends `customer_support.obj.core.escalation`

Requires `reason`


> An escalation here adds attention without moving ownership, so `reason` carries the whole payload: what specifically is stuck. "Customer is angry" convenes nobody useful. There is no receiving owner to name, which is exactly why contracts written against a tier ladder cannot be satisfied by this branch as written.


## Extends `customer_support.obj.core.knowledge_article`


> The swarm's output is a draft article whether anyone writes it or not. Treating knowledge as a downstream chore rather than the swarm's actual deliverable is the single most common reason this model gets more expensive over time instead of less.
